notes.front: What is cloud computing, as the international cloud vocabulary standard defines it?
notes.back: A way of giving network access to a scalable, elastic pool of shareable physical or virtual resources that users provision and administer themselves, on demand.
notes.explanation: The standard's examples of such resources include servers, operating systems, networks, software, applications and storage equipment.
notes.example: Like booking a hotel room online at any hour, except that what you book is servers and storage and you can change the booking yourself.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 3.2.5, PDF p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a cloud service customer (CSC)?
notes.back: A party that is in a business relationship for the purpose of using cloud services.
notes.explanation: The standard notes that this business relationship does not necessarily involve a financial agreement.
notes.example: A hospital that signs up for a hosted email service for its staff.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 3.2.11, PDF p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a cloud service provider (CSP)?
notes.back: A party that makes cloud services available.
notes.explanation: Its activities cover providing a cloud service, making sure it is delivered to the customer, and maintaining it.
notes.example: A company that runs data centres and rents out virtual servers by the hour.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.3, Cloud computing roles and activities, PDF p. 12
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a cloud service partner?
notes.back: A party that supports, or is auxiliary to, the activities of a cloud service provider, a cloud service customer, or both.
notes.explanation: What a partner does varies with the type of partner and its relationship with the provider and the customer.
notes.example: A training firm that teaches a customer's staff to use a provider's service.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.3, Cloud computing roles and activities, PDF p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a cloud service broker?
notes.back: A cloud service partner that negotiates relationships between cloud service customers and cloud service providers.
notes.explanation: The vocabulary standard defines the broker as a kind of partner, not as a role of its own.
notes.example: Like an estate agent who matches tenants with landlords.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 3.2.9, PDF p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a cloud auditor?
notes.back: A cloud service partner responsible for auditing the provision and use of cloud services.
notes.explanation: Like the broker, the vocabulary standard defines the auditor as a kind of partner.
notes.example: Like a financial auditor who checks a company's accounts, but checking how a cloud service is run.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 3.2.3, PDF p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a cloud carrier?
notes.back: An intermediary that provides connectivity and transport of cloud services from cloud providers to cloud consumers.
notes.explanation: It sits between the two parties: it carries the service rather than providing or using it.
notes.example: Like the postal service that carries a parcel from a shop to your door without selling you anything.
notes.source: NIST SP 500-292, NIST Cloud Computing Reference Architecture (2011), §2.1, Table 1: Actors in Cloud Computing, PDF p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: Cloud Carrier An intermediary that provides connectivity and transport of cloud services from Cloud Providers to Cloud Consumers.

notes.front: What is on-demand self-service?
notes.back: The customer provisions computing capabilities as needed, automatically or with minimal interaction with the provider.
notes.explanation: The standard says its focus is cutting the cost, time and effort needed to take an action.
notes.example: Like topping up a phone at a machine instead of queueing at a counter.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.2, Key characteristics, PDF p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is broad network access?
notes.back: Resources are available over a network and reached through standard mechanisms from many different kinds of client device.
notes.explanation: The standard's focus is convenience: users can reach resources from wherever they work, as long as the network reaches them.
notes.example: Opening the same online spreadsheet on a phone on the train and on a desktop at work.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.2, Key characteristics, PDF p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is multi-tenancy?
notes.back: Allocating resources so that several tenants, with their computations and data, are isolated from and inaccessible to one another.
notes.explanation: A tenant is one or more cloud service users who share access to a set of physical and virtual resources.
notes.example: Like flats in one building: shared walls and pipes, but each flat has its own lock.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clauses 3.2.27 and 3.2.37, PDF pp. 9 and 10
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is rapid elasticity and scalability?
notes.back: Physical or virtual resources can be adjusted quickly and elastically, sometimes automatically, to increase or decrease them.
notes.explanation: The standard's focus: customers no longer need to worry about limited resources and might not need capacity planning.
notes.example: Like a restaurant that can add tables the moment a coach party arrives and take them away afterwards.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.2, Key characteristics, PDF p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is resource pooling?
notes.back: Aggregating a provider's physical or virtual resources to serve one or more cloud service customers.
notes.explanation: The standard says pooling lets providers support multi-tenancy while abstraction hides the complexity from the customer.
notes.example: Like a car-sharing club whose members all draw on one common fleet.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.2, Key characteristics, PDF p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is measured service?
notes.back: Metered delivery of cloud services, so that usage can be monitored, controlled, reported and billed.
notes.explanation: The standard says its focus is that the customer may pay only for the resources it uses.
notes.example: Like a water meter, but counting storage and processing.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.2, Key characteristics, PDF p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is virtualisation?
notes.back: Simulating the software and/or hardware on which other software runs; the simulated environment is called a virtual machine.
notes.explanation: Virtualisation comes in many forms, told apart mainly by the layer of the computing architecture being simulated.
notes.example: Like a flight simulator: the pilot inside acts as if the aircraft were real.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-125, Guide to Security for Full Virtualization Technologies (2011), §2.1, Full Virtualization, PDF p. 10
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: Virtualization is the simulation of the software and/or hardware upon which other software runs. This simulated environment is called a virtual machine (VM). There are many forms of virtualization, distinguished primarily by computing architecture layer.

notes.front: In container platforms, what does orchestration do?
notes.back: It decides which containers run on which hosts, pulls the images they need and runs them with the resources specified.
notes.explanation: The orchestrator works from what it knows of every host in the cluster, including the resources each one has available.
notes.example: Like an air-traffic controller deciding which runway each aircraft uses.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-190, Application Container Security Guide (2017), §2.3, Container Technology Architecture, PDF p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: The orchestrator knows the state of each host within the cluster, including what resources are available for each host, and determines which containers will run on which hosts. The orchestrator then pulls the required images from the registry and runs them as containers with the designated resources.

notes.front: Special Publication 800-145 describes a cloud model made of {{c1::five}} essential characteristics, three service models and four deployment models.
notes.back: five
notes.explanation: Every part of the definition falls into one of these three groups.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing (2011), §2, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing, PDF p. 6
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: This cloud model is composed of five essential characteristics, three service models, and four deployment models.

notes.front: Under Special Publication 800-145, how are the shared pool's configurable computing resources provisioned and released?
notes.back: Rapidly, with minimal management effort or service provider interaction.
notes.explanation: The definition describes on-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable resources such as networks, servers, storage, applications and services.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing (2011), §2, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing, PDF p. 6
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: Cloud computing is a model for enabling ubiquitous, convenient, on-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources (e.g., networks, servers, storage, applications, and services) that can be rapidly provisioned and released with minimal management effort or service provider interaction.

notes.front: With whom is a cloud service customer's business relationship, in the vocabulary standard's description of roles?
notes.back: With a cloud service provider or a cloud service partner.
notes.explanation: The customer's key activities include using cloud services, performing business administration and administering its use of cloud services, among others.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.3, Cloud computing roles and activities, PDF p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two sub-roles that the cloud service provider role includes, according to the vocabulary standard?
notes.back: Any two, among others: business manager, service manager, network provider.
notes.explanation: The standard describes the provider as carrying an extensive set of activities and numerous sub-roles; security and risk manager is a fourth example.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.3, Cloud computing roles and activities, PDF p. 12
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Special Publication 500-292 groups a cloud provider's activities into five areas. What are two of them?
notes.back: Any two of the five, for example service deployment and service orchestration.
notes.explanation: The five areas are service deployment, service orchestration, cloud service management, security and privacy.
notes.source: NIST SP 500-292, NIST Cloud Computing Reference Architecture (2011), §2.3, Cloud Provider, PDF p. 14
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: a cloud provider conducts its activities in the areas of service deployment, service orchestration, cloud service management, security, and privacy.

notes.front: In the international reference architecture, which sub-role of cloud service partner designs, develops, tests and maintains the implementation of a cloud service?
notes.back: The cloud service developer.
notes.explanation: The reference architecture names three partner sub-roles: cloud service developer, cloud auditor and cloud service broker.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3502 | ISO/IEC 17789:2014, Cloud computing reference architecture, clause 8.4.1, Cloud service partner sub-roles, PDF p. 27
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the international reference architecture, during which phase of a cloud service does the cloud service broker act?
notes.back: Only during the contracting phase, between customer and provider; it is not involved while the service is consumed.
notes.explanation: Its activities are acquiring and assessing customers, assessing the marketplace and setting up the legal agreement.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3502 | ISO/IEC 17789:2014, Cloud computing reference architecture, clause 8.4.1.3, Cloud service broker, PDF p. 27
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which cloud broker service enhances a given service by improving a specific capability and adding value-added services?
notes.back: Service intermediation.
notes.explanation: Special Publication 500-292 gives managing access, identity management, performance reporting and enhanced security as examples of such improvements.
notes.source: NIST SP 500-292, NIST Cloud Computing Reference Architecture (2011), §2.5, Cloud Broker, PDF p. 15
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: Service Intermediation: A cloud broker enhances a given service by improving some specific capability and providing value-added services to cloud consumers. The improvement can be managing access to cloud services, identity management, performance reporting, enhanced security, etc.

notes.front: Which cloud broker service combines and integrates multiple services into one or more new services?
notes.back: Service aggregation.
notes.explanation: In aggregation the broker provides data integration and ensures secure data movement between the consumer and multiple providers.
notes.source: NIST SP 500-292, NIST Cloud Computing Reference Architecture (2011), §2.5, Cloud Broker, PDF p. 15
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: Service Aggregation: A cloud broker combines and integrates multiple services into one or more new services. The broker provides data integration and ensures the secure data movement between the cloud consumer and multiple cloud providers.

notes.front: Which cloud broker service is like aggregation, except that the services being combined are not fixed?
notes.back: Service arbitrage.
notes.explanation: Arbitrage gives the broker the flexibility to choose services from several sources, for example by using a credit-scoring service to pick the best-scoring one.
notes.source: NIST SP 500-292, NIST Cloud Computing Reference Architecture (2011), §2.5, Cloud Broker, PDF p. 15
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: Service arbitrage is similar to service aggregation except that the services being aggregated are not fixed. Service arbitrage means a broker has the flexibility to choose services from multiple agencies. The cloud broker, for example, can use a credit-scoring service to measure and select an agency with the best score.

notes.front: In the international reference architecture, what does a cloud audit typically cover?
notes.back: Operations, performance and security.
notes.explanation: The audit examines whether a specified set of audit criteria is met; the standard cites security criteria as one example of such a set.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3502 | ISO/IEC 17789:2014, Cloud computing reference architecture, clause 8.4.1.2, Cloud auditor, PDF p. 27
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In Special Publication 500-292, what is the aim of a cloud auditor's independent examination of cloud service controls?
notes.back: To express an opinion on them.
notes.explanation: Audits verify conformance to standards by reviewing objective evidence, and can assess a provider's security controls, privacy impact and performance.
notes.source: NIST SP 500-292, NIST Cloud Computing Reference Architecture (2011), §2.4, Cloud Auditor, PDF p. 15
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: A cloud auditor is a party that can perform an independent examination of cloud service controls with the intent to express an opinion thereon. Audits are performed to verify conformance to standards through review of objective evidence.

notes.front: Besides network and telecommunication carriers, who may distribute cloud services, according to Special Publication 500-292?
notes.back: A transport agent: a business that physically transports storage media such as high-capacity hard drives.
notes.explanation: Distribution of cloud services is normally done by network and telecommunication carriers or by such an agent.
notes.source: NIST SP 500-292, NIST Cloud Computing Reference Architecture (2011), §2.6, Cloud Carrier, PDF p. 16
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: The distribution of cloud services is normally provided by network and telecommunication carriers or a transport agent [8], where a transport agent refers to a business organization that provides physical transport of storage media such as high-capacity hard drives.

notes.front: The reference architecture in Special Publication 500-292 defines {{c1::five}} major actors: consumer, provider, carrier, auditor and broker.
notes.back: five
notes.explanation: Each actor is an entity, a person or an organisation, that takes part in a transaction or process or performs tasks in cloud computing.
notes.source: NIST SP 500-292, NIST Cloud Computing Reference Architecture (2011), §2.1, Overview, PDF p. 10
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: the NIST cloud computing reference architecture defines five major actors: cloud consumer, cloud provider, cloud carrier, cloud auditor and cloud broker. Each actor is an entity (a person or an organization) that participates in a transaction or process and/or performs tasks in cloud computing.

notes.front: Which actor in Special Publication 500-292 maintains a business relationship with, and uses service from, cloud providers?
notes.back: The cloud consumer.
notes.explanation: The table of actors gives each of the five a one-line definition; this is the consumer's, the party the services are for.
notes.source: NIST SP 500-292, NIST Cloud Computing Reference Architecture (2011), §2.1, Table 1: Actors in Cloud Computing, PDF p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: Cloud Consumer A person or organization that maintains a business relationship with, and uses service from, Cloud Providers.

notes.front: How many roles does the international reference architecture define?
notes.back: Three: cloud service customer, cloud service provider and cloud service partner.
notes.explanation: Parties such as brokers, auditors and developers appear as sub-roles of the partner, not as roles of their own.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3502 | ISO/IEC 17789:2014, Cloud computing reference architecture, clause 7.2.2, Roles and sub-roles, PDF p. 12
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: According to the vocabulary standard, what may limit whether a public cloud service is actually available to a particular customer?
notes.back: Jurisdictional regulations.
notes.explanation: A public cloud is potentially open to any customer, but the law where that customer sits can still restrict its use.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.5, Cloud deployment models, PDF p. 12
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: According to the vocabulary standard, what can statutory, regulatory and legal requirements change for customers and providers?
notes.back: The responsibilities of both cloud service customers and cloud service providers.
notes.explanation: These requirements vary by market sector and by jurisdiction, and complying with them is often tied to governance and risk management.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.6, Cloud computing cross cutting aspects (Regulatory), PDF p. 14
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: The international vocabulary standard lists {{c1::six}} key characteristics of cloud computing.
notes.back: six
notes.explanation: They are broad network access, measured service, multi-tenancy, on-demand self-service, rapid elasticity and scalability, and resource pooling.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.2, Key characteristics, PDF p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: According to the vocabulary standard, can one cloud service customer hold several tenancies with a single provider?
notes.back: Yes, for example one for each of several groups within the organisation.
notes.explanation: Typically the users forming a tenant all belong to the same customer organisation, though in public and community clouds a tenant may mix users from several customers.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.2, Key characteristics (Multi-tenancy), PDF p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Under Special Publication 800-145, how do the capabilities available for provisioning often appear to the consumer?
notes.back: Unlimited, and obtainable in any quantity at any time.
notes.explanation: Capabilities can be provisioned and released elastically, sometimes automatically, to scale outward and inward with demand.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing (2011), §2, Essential Characteristics (Rapid elasticity), PDF p. 6
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: Capabilities can be elastically provisioned and released, in some cases automatically, to scale rapidly outward and inward commensurate with demand. To the consumer, the capabilities available for provisioning often appear to be unlimited and can be appropriated in any quantity at any time.

notes.front: Under Special Publication 800-145, what control does a customer generally have over where pooled resources are located?
notes.back: No control or knowledge of the exact location, though it may be able to choose at a higher level, such as country or data centre.
notes.explanation: The definition calls this a sense of location independence.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing (2011), §2, Essential Characteristics (Resource pooling), PDF p. 6
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: There is a sense of location independence in that the customer generally has no control or knowledge over the exact location of the provided resources but may be able to specify location at a higher level of abstraction (e.g., country, state, or datacenter).

notes.front: Under Special Publication 800-145, for whom does measured service provide transparency?
notes.back: For both the provider and the consumer of the service.
notes.explanation: Resource usage can be monitored, controlled and reported, and metering is typically done on a pay-per-use or charge-per-use basis.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing (2011), §2, Essential Characteristics (Measured service), PDF p. 6
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: Resource usage can be monitored, controlled, and reported, providing transparency for both the provider and consumer of the utilized service.

notes.front: In full virtualisation, what does the hypervisor, also called the virtual machine monitor, control?
notes.back: The flow of instructions between the guest operating systems and the physical hardware.
notes.explanation: It can also partition the system's resources and isolate the guest operating systems so that each has access only to its own resources.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-125, Guide to Security for Full Virtualization Technologies (2011), §2.1, Full Virtualization, PDF p. 10
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: The guest OSs on a host are managed by the hypervisor, also called the virtual machine monitor (VMM), which controls the flow of instructions between the guest OSs and the physical hardware, such as CPU, disk storage, memory, and network interface cards. The hypervisor can partition the system’s resources and isolate the guest OSs

notes.front: In bare metal (native) virtualisation, where does the hypervisor run?
notes.back: Directly on the underlying hardware, with no host operating system.
notes.explanation: The hypervisor can even be built into the computer's firmware.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-125, Guide to Security for Full Virtualization Technologies (2011), §2.2, Types of Full Virtualization, PDF p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: In bare metal virtualization, also known as native virtualization, the hypervisor runs directly on the underlying hardware, without a host OS; the hypervisor can even be built into the computer’s firmware.

notes.front: In hosted virtualisation, where does the hypervisor run?
notes.back: On top of a host operating system.
notes.explanation: The host can be almost any common operating system, such as Windows, Linux or MacOS.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-125, Guide to Security for Full Virtualization Technologies (2011), §2.2, Types of Full Virtualization, PDF p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: known as hosted virtualization, the hypervisor runs on top of the host OS; the host OS can be almost any common operating system such as Windows, Linux, or MacOS.

notes.front: According to Special Publication 800-125, what can happen when many systems are combined onto a single physical computer?
notes.back: A security compromise can have a larger impact.
notes.explanation: The guide lists this among the negative security implications of full virtualisation, along with the extra layers of technology to manage.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-125, Guide to Security for Full Virtualization Technologies (2011), §2.1, Full Virtualization, PDF p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: Full virtualization has some negative security implications. Virtualization adds layers of technology, which can increase the security management burden by necessitating additional security controls. Also, combining many systems onto a single physical computer can cause a larger impact if a security compromise occurs.

notes.front: According to Special Publication 800-190, what may an orchestrator do if a host running containers fails?
notes.back: Automatically restart the containers on new hosts, depending on its configuration.
notes.explanation: Orchestration tools also monitor container resource use, job execution and machine health across hosts.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-190, Application Container Security Guide (2017), §2.3, Container Technology Architecture, PDF p. 22
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: Orchestration tools are also responsible for monitoring container resource consumption, job execution, and machine health across hosts. Depending on its configuration, an orchestrator may automatically restart containers on new hosts if the hosts they were initially running on failed.

notes.front: An insurer's contract lets an independent firm examine its provider's security controls and report on whether they meet an agreed set of criteria. Which role does the firm play?
notes.back: B: cloud auditor.
notes.choices:
A) Cloud service broker
B) Cloud auditor
C) Cloud service provider
notes.choicesExplained: A negotiates relationships between customers and providers; it does not assess controls. C makes services available and would be the party audited, not the auditor.
notes.explanation: Auditing the provision and use of cloud services against criteria is exactly the auditor's job, and the auditor is a kind of cloud service partner.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 3.2.3, PDF p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A firm helps a customer choose between three providers and negotiates the contract, then steps away once the service is in use. Which role fits it best?
notes.back: B: cloud service broker.
notes.choices:
A) Cloud carrier
B) Cloud service broker
C) Cloud auditor
notes.choicesExplained: A provides connectivity and transport of services, not negotiation. C examines services and controls; it does not arrange contracts.
notes.explanation: Negotiating relationships between customers and providers, and acting only while the deal is made, is how the standards describe the broker.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3502 | ISO/IEC 17789:2014, Cloud computing reference architecture, clause 8.4.1.3, Cloud service broker, PDF p. 27
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A mobile network operator provides the links over which a firm's staff reach their provider's services. Which actor of Special Publication 500-292 is the operator?
notes.back: B: cloud carrier.
notes.choices:
A) Cloud service provider
B) Cloud carrier
C) Cloud service broker
notes.choicesExplained: A makes the service itself available; the operator only carries it. C manages use and delivery and negotiates relationships; the operator does neither.
notes.explanation: The carrier provides connectivity and transport of cloud services between providers and consumers.
notes.source: NIST SP 500-292, NIST Cloud Computing Reference Architecture (2011), §2.1, Table 1: Actors in Cloud Computing, PDF p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: Cloud Carrier An intermediary that provides connectivity and transport of cloud services from Cloud Providers to Cloud Consumers.

notes.front: Each month a broker checks a rating service and moves a customer's workload to whichever storage offer scores best. Which broker service is this?
notes.back: A: service arbitrage.
notes.choices:
A) Service arbitrage
B) Service aggregation
C) Service intermediation
notes.choicesExplained: B combines a fixed set of services into a new one. C improves a single given service, for example by adding identity management.
notes.explanation: In arbitrage the services being combined are not fixed: the broker is free to choose among several sources, for instance by score.
notes.source: NIST SP 500-292, NIST Cloud Computing Reference Architecture (2011), §2.5, Cloud Broker, PDF p. 15
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: Service arbitrage is similar to service aggregation except that the services being aggregated are not fixed. Service arbitrage means a broker has the flexibility to choose services from multiple agencies.

notes.front: At 2 a.m. a developer creates a new virtual server from the provider's web portal, and nobody at the provider is involved. Which key characteristic is this?
notes.back: C: on-demand self-service.
notes.choices:
A) Resource pooling
B) Measured service
C) On-demand self-service
notes.choicesExplained: B is about metering and billing use, not who starts provisioning. A is about the provider aggregating resources for many customers.
notes.explanation: The customer provisions capabilities as needed, automatically or with minimal interaction with the provider.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.2, Key characteristics, PDF p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An online shop's servers grow from 10 to 200 during a weekend sale and shrink back on Monday, without the shop buying hardware. Which key characteristic is this?
notes.back: B: rapid elasticity and scalability.
notes.choices:
A) Broad network access
B) Rapid elasticity and scalability
C) Multi-tenancy
notes.choicesExplained: A is about reaching resources from many kinds of device. C is about keeping tenants isolated from one another.
notes.explanation: Resources are adjusted quickly, up and down, sometimes automatically, so the shop need not plan for peak capacity.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.2, Key characteristics, PDF p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A customer's invoice lists exactly how many gigabyte-months of storage and hours of processing it used. Which key characteristic makes this possible?
notes.back: A: measured service.
notes.choices:
A) Measured service
B) On-demand self-service
C) Rapid elasticity and scalability
notes.choicesExplained: B lets the customer provision without help but says nothing about metering. C lets resources grow and shrink; billing needs metering.
notes.explanation: Metered delivery lets usage be monitored, controlled, reported and billed, so the customer pays for what it uses.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.2, Key characteristics, PDF p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Two rival banks run workloads on the same provider's physical servers, and neither can see the other's data or processing. Which key characteristic is at work?
notes.back: B: multi-tenancy.
notes.choices:
A) Measured service
B) Multi-tenancy
C) Broad network access
notes.choicesExplained: A is about metering use. C is about reaching resources over the network from many devices; neither isolates tenants.
notes.explanation: Multi-tenancy allocates resources so that tenants and their computations and data are isolated from and inaccessible to one another.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 3.2.27, PDF p. 9
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A customer can choose that its data stays in Germany, but cannot see which building or disk holds it. Which characteristic in Special Publication 800-145 describes this?
notes.back: A: resource pooling.
notes.choices:
A) Resource pooling
B) On-demand self-service
C) Measured service
notes.choicesExplained: B is about provisioning without human interaction. C is about monitoring and reporting usage, not where resources sit.
notes.explanation: Pooling brings a sense of location independence: no control over the exact location, but perhaps a choice at a higher level such as country.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing (2011), §2, Essential Characteristics (Resource pooling), PDF p. 6
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: There is a sense of location independence in that the customer generally has no control or knowledge over the exact location of the provided resources but may be able to specify location at a higher level of abstraction (e.g., country, state, or datacenter).

notes.front: A city council signs an agreement to use a hosted records service run by a company. Which role does the council play?
notes.back: C: cloud service customer.
notes.choices:
A) Cloud service partner
B) Cloud service provider
C) Cloud service customer
notes.choicesExplained: B is the company that makes the service available. A supports the provider's or customer's activities rather than using the service itself.
notes.explanation: It is the party in a business relationship for the purpose of using cloud services; the company is the provider.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 3.2.11, PDF p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A company runs data centres and sells hosted databases that anyone can sign up for. Which role does it play?
notes.back: A: cloud service provider.
notes.choices:
A) Cloud service provider
B) Cloud service broker
C) Cloud carrier
notes.choicesExplained: B negotiates between customers and providers without providing the service. C carries services over networks; it does not make them available.
notes.explanation: Making cloud services available is what defines the provider.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 3.2.15, PDF p. 9
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A software house is contracted to design, build and test a component that a provider will sell as part of its cloud service. In the international reference architecture, what role and sub-role does it play?
notes.back: B: cloud service partner, as cloud service developer.
notes.choices:
A) Cloud service customer
B) Cloud service partner, as cloud service developer
C) Cloud service partner, as cloud service broker
notes.choicesExplained: A uses cloud services; the software house builds part of one. C negotiates relationships between customers and providers.
notes.explanation: The developer is the partner sub-role that designs, develops, tests and maintains a cloud service's implementation.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3502 | ISO/IEC 17789:2014, Cloud computing reference architecture, clause 8.4.1.1, Cloud service developer, PDF p. 27
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A hosting firm offers servers over the internet, but each new server needs a ticket and two weeks of manual work by its staff. Which essential characteristic of Special Publication 800-145 is missing?
notes.back: C: on-demand self-service.
notes.choices:
A) Measured service
B) Broad network access
C) On-demand self-service
notes.choicesExplained: B is present: the servers are offered over the network. A concerns metering use; nothing suggests it is missing.
notes.explanation: That characteristic requires provisioning as needed, automatically, without human interaction with each service provider.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing (2011), §2, Essential Characteristics (On-demand self-service), PDF p. 6
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: A consumer can unilaterally provision computing capabilities, such as server time and network storage, as needed automatically without requiring human interaction with each service provider.

notes.front: A checklist gives the five essential characteristics of Special Publication 800-145. Which characteristic must be added to match the six key characteristics of the international vocabulary standard?
notes.back: Multi-tenancy.
notes.explanation: The international standard lists multi-tenancy as a key characteristic in its own right; the other five appear on both lists.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3500 | ISO/IEC 17788:2014, Cloud computing: Overview and vocabulary, clause 6.2, Key characteristics, PDF p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An analyst wants to run a test virtual machine on her laptop while still using her normal browser and email beside it. Which form of full virtualisation suits this?
notes.back: A: hosted virtualisation.
notes.choices:
A) Hosted virtualisation
B) Bare metal virtualisation
notes.choicesExplained: B runs the hypervisor directly on the hardware and can only run applications inside virtualised systems, so her browser and email could not run beside it.
notes.explanation: Hosted virtualisation lets users run applications such as browsers and email clients alongside the virtualisation application.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-125, Guide to Security for Full Virtualization Technologies (2011), §2.2, Types of Full Virtualization, PDF p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: Hosted virtualization architectures also allow users to run applications such as web browsers and email clients alongside the hosted virtualization application, unlike bare metal architectures, which can only run applications within virtualized systems.

notes.front: A government agency maintains a business relationship with a provider and uses its analytics service. Which actor of Special Publication 500-292 is the agency?
notes.back: C: cloud consumer.
notes.choices:
A) Cloud auditor
B) Cloud broker
C) Cloud consumer
notes.choicesExplained: B manages use and delivery and negotiates for others; the agency uses the service itself. A assesses services independently.
notes.explanation: The consumer is the person or organisation that maintains a business relationship with, and uses service from, cloud providers.
notes.source: NIST SP 500-292, NIST Cloud Computing Reference Architecture (2011), §2.1, Table 1: Actors in Cloud Computing, PDF p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: Cloud Consumer A person or organization that maintains a business relationship with, and uses service from, Cloud Providers.

notes.front: A firm audits a provider's service. Under the international reference architecture, which role does the firm play?
notes.back: A: cloud service partner, in its cloud auditor sub-role.
notes.choices:
A) Cloud service partner, in its cloud auditor sub-role
B) A fourth role, cloud auditor
C) Cloud service customer
notes.choicesExplained: B does not exist: the international architecture has only three roles. C uses services; the firm assesses them.
notes.explanation: The international architecture has only three roles; the auditor is a sub-role of the partner.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3502 | ISO/IEC 17789:2014, Cloud computing reference architecture, clause 8.4.1.2, Cloud auditor, PDF p. 27
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Where does Special Publication 800-145 put multi-tenancy, given that it is not one of its five essential characteristics?
notes.back: Inside resource pooling: the provider's resources are pooled to serve multiple consumers using a multi-tenant model.
notes.explanation: The international vocabulary standard instead lists multi-tenancy as a sixth characteristic of its own.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing (2011), §2, Essential Characteristics (Resource pooling), PDF p. 6
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: The provider’s computing resources are pooled to serve multiple consumers using a multi-tenant model, with different physical and virtual resources dynamically assigned and reassigned according to consumer demand.

notes.front: How do the international reference architecture and Special Publication 500-292 differ in where they place the broker and the auditor?
notes.back: Internationally they are sub-roles of cloud service partner; Special Publication 500-292 lists them as actors in their own right.
notes.explanation: The international architecture defines only three roles, customer, provider and partner, and hangs broker, auditor and developer beneath the partner.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3502 | ISO/IEC 17789:2014, Cloud computing reference architecture, clause 8.4.1, Cloud service partner sub-roles, PDF p. 27
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does the broker in the international reference architecture differ from the broker in Special Publication 500-292?
notes.back: The international broker only negotiates during contracting; the 500-292 broker also manages use, performance and delivery, and may combine services.
notes.explanation: The international text says its broker is not itself a provider and is not involved while the service is consumed.
notes.source: ITU-T Y.3502 | ISO/IEC 17789:2014, Cloud computing reference architecture, clause 8.4.1.3, Cloud service broker, PDF p. 27; NIST SP 500-292, §2.1 Table 1 and §2.5, PDF pp. 11 and 15
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What can users do under hosted virtualisation that bare metal virtualisation does not allow?
notes.back: Run applications such as web browsers and email clients alongside the virtualisation application.
notes.explanation: Bare metal architectures can run applications only within virtualised systems.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-125, Guide to Security for Full Virtualization Technologies (2011), §2.2, Types of Full Virtualization, PDF p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: Hosted virtualization architectures also allow users to run applications such as web browsers and email clients alongside the hosted virtualization application, unlike bare metal architectures, which can only run applications within virtualized systems.

notes.front: How does Special Publication 800-190 contrast containers with traditional virtual machines over their lifetime?
notes.back: Containers should be deployed but not changed, and are replaced when updated; virtual machines are usually reconfigured and upgraded throughout their life.
notes.explanation: The guide calls immutability a fundamental operational difference between containers and hardware virtualisation.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-190, Application Container Security Guide (2017), §2.2, Containers, PDF p. 16
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: Immutability is a fundamental operational difference between containers and hardware virtualization. Traditional VMs are typically run as stateful entities that are deployed, reconfigured, and upgraded throughout their life.
